summary: Sugarbush (Rat Lake) Hill: CCC wooden tower built 1938, later steel Aermotor-style lookout; removed; only four footings remain on Potawatomi land.

facts.design: Last lookout a steel stairway-style tower, likely an Aermotor MC-39 (FFLOS). The 1938 CCC tower was wooden, 101 ft 6 in tall (FFLOS).
facts.status_note: FFLOS says only four footings of the last tower remain at the site.
facts.agency: Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources (administrator per FFLOS); Forest County Potawatomi (property owners per FFLOS)

access.note: Land belongs to the Forest County Potawatomi per FFLOS. Wikipedia says the peak is on their reservation and considered sacred. No source describes visiting rules.

visit.trail_note: No tower stands on the site, per FFLOS.

events.note: Civilian Conservation Corps built a wooden tower, 101 ft 6 in tall, in January and February 1938, replacing a steel first lookout under 100 ft. The later steel tower has no recorded date.
Clyde H. Spencer, chairman of the town of Lincoln, held an 11-day sit-down atop the tower, March 2 to 13, to press for reopened fire lanes to Forest County lakes
Wisconsin Historical Society placed a historical marker near the hill, per Wikipedia
FFLOS 'Removed' field reads 'circa 1980s'. 1980 is only a sorting placeholder; no source gives that year (see corrections).

evidence.supports: three lookout towers since the 30s; second-highest elevation in the state
evidence.quote: At the second highest elevation in the state, Sugar Bush Hill has housed three fire lookout towers since the 30’s

evidence.supports: first lookout was a steel structure under 100 ft
evidence.quote: The first lookout was a steel structure with a cab less than 100’ tall.

evidence.supports: wooden tower 101 ft 6 in built January and February 1938 by the CCC
evidence.quote: It was replaced by a wooden tower 101’ 6” tall built in January and February of 1938 by the Civilian Conservation Corps.

evidence.supports: later steel stairway tower, likely an Aermotor MC-39
evidence.quote: At an unknown later date the wooden structure was replaced with a steel stairway style tower, likely an Aermotor MC-39.

evidence.supports: lookout and radio link for WI DNR until late 1980s or early 1990s
evidence.quote: Rat Lake served as a lookout and radio link for the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources until the late 80’s or early 90’s.

evidence.supports: deemed unnecessary because adjacent lookouts covered the area
evidence.quote: It was deemed unnecessary at that time as the seen area from other adjacent lookouts covered most of the surrounding area.

evidence.supports: only four footings of the last tower remain
evidence.quote: Today, all that remains of the lookouts and the communications tower are the four footings of the Aermotor style tower which was the last lookout to occupy the site.

evidence.supports: Forest County Potawatomi as property owners

evidence.quote: Clyde H. Spencer ended his 11-day sitdown atop a 110-foot fire tower late yesterday

evidence.supports: Spencer in an eight-foot cubicle atop the tower
evidence.quote: the eight-foot cubicle atop the 110-foot forest fire lookout tower on Sugarbush hill

evidence.supports: climbed March 2 to plead for fire lanes to be reopened
evidence.quote: climbed the lofty tower on Sugar Bush Hill March 2 to dramatize his plea that fire lanes be reopened by the State Conservation Commission

evidence.supports: 1939 Wisconsin State Journal gave the tower as 110 ft
evidence.quote: In 1939, the Wisconsin State Journal stated that the tower was 110 ft (34 m) tall.
The tower has since been removed.

evidence.supports: land on Forest County Potawatomi reservation, considered sacred
evidence.quote: The land is on the Forest County Potawatomi Indian Reservation and it is considered sacred.

evidence.supports: 1956 Wisconsin Historical Society marker near the hill
evidence.quote: In 1956, the Wisconsin Historical Society placed a historical marker near the hill.
People suspected that the sitdown strike was a publicity stunt

corrections.why: FFLOS gives only 'circa 1980s', and the same page says the lookout was in use into the late 1980s or early 1990s, so no single year is supported.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: FFLOS gives 101 ft 6 in (about 30.9 m) for the 1938 wooden tower. 1939 newspapers quoted by centraluslookouts and Wikipedia say 110 ft (about 34 m). The record keeps 33.5 m, the newspaper figure; the sources do not reconcile the two.
FFLOS dates removal to circa 1980s but says the lookout served into the late 1980s or early 1990s. Wikipedia gives no date for removal.

notes_for_editor: The 1939 newspaper quotes come second-hand from centraluslookouts and were not checked against the papers. Wikipedia's own sources were not opened. Height conflict (101 ft 6 in vs 110 ft) left open. Access 'private' is inferred from the owner listing; no visiting rules found. Brief's 1980 removal year is more precise than the source.
